sessions: Right so. My sister in Boston swears by you for keeping her life in order, and mine is currently held together by sticky notes on the fridge and a calendar the kids have drawn on, so here we are. Liam. Galway. Secondary school teacher, geography and history, 16 years at it. Also do furniture restoration on the side, which started as a hobby and is now somehow a small business called Driftwood Restoration.

First a teaching thing, because it's the end of August and I'm in denial about September. I'm doing a first year history class on "how do we know about the past" — sources, archaeology, that craic. Can you give me a starter activity for the very first lesson that isn't "write down three facts about yourself"? I want something that makes 12 year olds actually think.
The "rubbish bin archaeology" one is class. Give them a bag of (clean) rubbish from a fictional family and they have to work out who lives there. I'll do that. I'll make the bag myself, God help me.
What would you put in the bag? I want a few red herrings in there too.
Ha, the receipt for 14 tins of cat food and a dog lead is a nice red herring. Grand.

Bit of context on me so you're not lost later. I'm separated, two kids: Saoirse is 13, Cian is 9. Their mam Niamh moved to Dublin two years ago with work, so the kids live with me in Knocknacarra during the week and go to her every second weekend. It works, mostly. Saoirse is 13 going on 35 and Cian is 9 going on golden retriever.

Also two things you should know if you're ever planning my week: I don't work Sundays. Not school stuff, not Driftwood, nothing. Sunday is the kids' day, or my day when they're in Dublin. I've broken that rule before and it doesn't end well. And I'm pescatarian, been off meat 10 years, fish is fine. The kids eat everything, Cian would eat a chair leg if you put ketchup on it.

Ok, a quick one: what's the difference between a primary and secondary source when it comes to photographs? A kid asked me last year if a photo of the Famine was a primary source and I fumbled it because there basically aren't any photos of the Famine.

Right, so a photograph from the time is primary, but a later photo of a Famine site or a staged image is secondary, and the lack of photographs is itself a teaching point about whose story gets recorded. Grand, that's a lesson in itself.
Thanks, that'll do me for tonight. Cian wants me to watch him do keepy-uppies for the 400th time.
Back. Two Driftwood bits and some family admin.

So the van. I've been doing deliveries for Driftwood with a borrowed trailer from my neighbour Pádraig and it's getting embarrassing. I'm saving for a small used van, something like a Transit Connect or a Berlingo. Budget around 9 grand. What should I look out for buying second hand in Ireland? NCT, mileage, all that.
Good list. The "ask if it was ever a courier van" tip is a good one, those things have done the distance of the moon.

Second thing, Driftwood. I've a new commission that's my biggest yet. A couple in Oranmore, the Kellys, Maeve and Donal, have a 1920s oak sideboard that was her grandmother's and six matching dining chairs. The sideboard's top has water damage and a big chunk of veneer has lifted and some of it's missing, and the chairs need re-gluing and new seats. They want it all done properly, French polish, the works.

The problem is the veneer. I need quarter-sawn oak veneer that matches the figure on the original, and the only place that has proper stuff is Murphy Timber in Cork. I ordered it and they've told me 3 to 4 weeks because they're waiting on a delivery from their supplier. Can't do the top without it. Everything else on the sideboard depends on the top being done first, really.
How long does French polishing take on a piece that size, realistically? The Kellys asked and I said "a while" which is apparently not an answer.
Right, so many thin coats over several days with drying time, and you can't rush it in a cold workshop. A good week or more of polishing for the sideboard alone. I'll tell them that.

Family admin: Saoirse is getting braces. Finally. She's been waiting a year on the HSE list and then Niamh and I just said feck it and went private. Orthodontist is Dr. Coyne on Shop Street. Fitting is booked for 18 November. She's mortified about it, she's already practising smiling with her mouth closed.
How do I convince a 13 year old that braces aren't the end of the world? Everything I say is apparently "cringe".
Ha, "don't say anything, just get her the fancy coloured bands and let her friends do the convincing". That's probably right. Teenagers listen to everyone except their father.
Right, that's me. Thanks.
Evening. School stuff, the big one.

I'm leading the Transition Year trip to Berlin this year. It's my second time doing it, first was 2019 before Covid wrecked everything. 44 students signed up so far, which is a lot. Dates are 19 to 23 March next year. Five days, four nights.
My co-leader is Aoife Brennan, she teaches German, which is very handy because my German consists of "zwei Bier bitte" and "Entschuldigung" which I mostly use in the wrong order.

The thing holding everything up is the Board of Management. Any overseas trip has to be approved by the Board and they only meet once a month. The September meeting got postponed, so it's not approved yet. I can't take deposits from parents until it's approved, and the tour company needs deposits to hold the flights.
The tour operator is EuroStudy Tours, the woman dealing with us is Hannah Kiely. She sent the quote, I'll upload it, so you have the numbers.

Can you help me write the info letter to parents? It should explain the trip, the cost, that it's pending Board approval, and that deposits will only be collected after approval. Not too long, parents don't read past paragraph two.
Good. Can you make it a bit warmer at the start and put the cost in bold? Parents always ask "how much" first and you can't blame them.

Perfect. One more thing: what should a TY trip to Berlin include history-wise that's appropriate for 15 and 16 year olds? We have the Bundestag and Sachsenhausen in the quote, I want to prepare them properly for Sachsenhausen in particular.

That's really thoughtful. The pre-visit lesson on "how do we remember difficult history" ties in nicely with what I do with the Famine anyway. I might do a Famine memorial / Berlin memorial comparison.

Also, unrelated but on my mind. My dad died two years ago this November. He used to walk the prom in Salthill every single day, rain or shine. Me and my brothers want to put a memorial bench on the prom with a plaque. You apply to Galway City Council. I've the form half filled in. Is there a typical wording for these plaques? I don't want it to be soppy, Dad would haunt me.
"In memory of Mattie O'Driscoll, who walked this prom every day and never once agreed it was too cold" — that's him exactly. Brilliant. I'll run it past my brothers.
Right, uploading the EuroStudy quote now.
Grand, you have the EuroStudy thing. Bit of school politics today, sorry in advance.

Our principal, Tom Hennessy, announced at the staff meeting that he's retiring at Christmas. He's been principal for 14 years. Lovely man, a bit old school, terrified of email. We all knew it was coming but it's still a shock.

The new principal has already been appointed: Gráinne Walsh. She's currently deputy principal in a school in Athenry. She starts in January. So Tom's still the boss until the Christmas holidays and then it's Gráinne from January.
I've met her once at a CPD day. Very sharp, very big on "data-informed decision making", which I'm told means more spreadsheets. Staffroom is nervous.

For the Berlin trip that's actually a bit awkward because Tom approved the idea in principle, but Gráinne will be principal when we actually go in March. Should I be keeping her in the loop already? How do I do that without stepping on Tom's toes?
Yeah, a short courtesy email after the Board approves, cc'ing Tom, framed as "so you're aware of what's coming". Sound.

Different topic. One of my Leaving Cert geography students sent me her draft for the geographical investigation (the fieldwork project) and I'm not allowed to write it for her, obviously, but I can give general feedback. Here's her introduction, tell me what general advice you'd give without rewriting it:

"For my geographical investigation I decided to investigate the coastal processes at Silver Strand beach in Barna. I chose this topic because I live near the beach and I have always been interested in how beaches change over time. I want to find out if there is longshore drift at Silver Strand and if the beach profile changes from one end to the other. I will measure the beach profile at three sites using ranging poles and a clinometer and I will measure the size of the pebbles using a ruler. I will also do a float test to see the direction of longshore drift. I think that longshore drift will be from west to east because the prevailing winds in Ireland are south westerly. I think that the beach will be steeper at the end with bigger pebbles."

Good. So: turn the "I want to find out" into clear numbered hypotheses, justify the site choice with something more than "I live near it", mention sampling (how many pebbles per site), and say how she'll control for the tide. That's general enough that I can say it to the whole class.

Cheers. Also, random one, what's the actual difference between a "sound" and a "bay" geographically? Cian asked me why it's Galway Bay but the Blasket Sound and I said "tradition" which is the coward's answer.

Right, a sound is a narrow channel between two bodies of land usually, and a bay is a broad indentation of the coast. So the Blasket Sound is between the mainland and the islands. Grand, I'll redeem myself tomorrow.
Night.
Howya. Driftwood is getting busy, which is great and also terrifying.

Second commission landed this week. Orla, who owns Cupán, the little café on the Salthill end of the prom, wants four benches for the window seating. She saw a bench I did for a friend's porch on Instagram. Here's her email, she's very enthusiastic:

"Hi Liam!! Orla from Cupán here, I got your number from Sinéad (Joe's wife, the porch bench!!). Ok so I am DESPERATE for new seating in the front window, the current benches are flat pack from 2015 and one of them squeaks so loud the customers think it's a seagull. I'm looking for 4 benches, each about 140cm long, to go along the big front window. I'd love them to be in a light wood, oak or ash, with a natural look, nothing too shiny, more matt. They need to be really durable because we get families with buggies and toddlers climbing everything and the odd wet dog. Would love a slightly rounded edge on the front so nobody bangs their shins. Height about 46cm with cushions on top (I'll get the cushions made separately). I would LOVE them before the Christmas rush, so ideally by mid-November? Budget wise I was thinking around 1,600 for all 4 but tell me if I'm being mad. Also is it possible to do some kind of storage underneath? Even just an open shelf for high chairs or toys? Thanks a million, I'm so excited!! Orla x"

I've told her 1,600 is a bit tight for oak with storage, I said 1,950 for ash with an open shelf underneath, and she said yes straight away, which means I probably undercharged. Classic. Delivery agreed for 20 November.
Ash vs oak for café benches that'll get abused by toddlers and dogs. Ash is cheaper, is it tough enough?
Grand, ash is plenty tough, and the key is the finish. I'll think about finish later, she wants matt.

So now there's "the bench" for Dad on the prom and "the benches" for Cupán, also on the prom. I said "the bench is coming along" to my brother and he thought I meant Dad's one. I need to name things better. Cupán benches are Driftwood work, Dad's bench is the council one, the bench itself comes from the council's approved supplier, I'm not making it.
Quick technical one: what's the best glue for re-gluing old dining chair joints that were originally done with hide glue? The Kelly chairs.
Right, hot hide glue or liquid hide glue so it's reversible and compatible with the old glue, don't use PVA on antique joints. That's what I thought, good to have it confirmed.
How do I clean out the old glue from the mortises without damaging them? Some of these joints are a hundred years old.
Warm water and vinegar, patience, and a sharpened scraper. Grand. Patience is the hard bit.
The Kellys signed the agreement, I'll upload it. Maeve is lovely but she changes her mind a lot, so I wrote everything down.
Right, off to the workshop for an hour while the kids are at swimming.
Evening. Landlord drama and a marking question.

So my workshop. I rent a unit in a little craft yard in Ballybane, Unit 6. The yard was owned for years by Pat Flaherty, an old farmer who never raised the rent, never fixed anything, and once paid me in a bag of potatoes when I fixed his kitchen table. Pat's sold the whole yard. New owner is a property company, Corrib Lettings. They've taken over from this month and my contact is now a woman called Sinéad Moran. Not the same Sinéad as Orla's friend, Galway is about 40% Sinéads.
Sinéad's sent an email saying a formal lease renewal letter is coming and that there'll be "updated terms". I've been paying Pat 620 a month for six years. I'm braced.
What are my rights as a commercial tenant in Ireland if the new owner wants to change terms? I know residential tenants have the RTB but I don't think that covers workshops.

Right, commercial is mostly about what's in the lease, and after 5 years continuous occupation I might have some renewal rights under the Landlord and Tenant Act unless I signed a renunciation. I never signed anything with Pat, he did everything on a handshake. Interesting. I'll wait and see what's in the letter.
Also the Kellys paid the deposit, 1,140, so that's in the bank. First time Driftwood's had a deposit that size, felt very grown up.

Marking question. I've a TY class doing a short essay on "Was the 1916 Rising a success?" and I want a simple rubric so I mark consistently. Here's one of the essays so you can see the level:

"The 1916 Rising was a rebellion against British rule in Ireland that happened at Easter 1916. It was led by people like Patrick Pearse and James Connolly. They took over the GPO and other buildings in Dublin and Pearse read the Proclamation. The British army came and there was fighting for six days and a lot of Dublin was destroyed. In the end the rebels surrendered because they were outnumbered. At the time most people in Dublin were angry at the rebels because their city was destroyed and lots of people were killed including civilians. So in the short term it was not a success because they lost. But then the British executed the leaders, 15 of them, in Kilmainham Gaol, and this made people change their minds and feel sorry for the rebels. In the 1918 election Sinn Féin won most of the seats in Ireland. Then there was the War of Independence and in 1922 the Irish Free State was created. So in the long term I think the Rising was a success because it led to independence. But some people say that it caused a lot of violence and maybe Ireland would have got Home Rule anyway without it. I think it was a success because without it Ireland would not be free."

That's a solid rubric. Four bands, and I like that "acknowledges counter-argument" is its own criterion, because this kid did that and should get credit for it even though the conclusion is a bit flat.
Can you write feedback for this specific essay using the rubric? Two strengths, one thing to improve. Kind but honest.

Perfect. "Your paragraph on public opinion changing after the executions is the strongest part — now push your conclusion to engage with the Home Rule argument you raised, rather than just restating your opinion." That's exactly what I'd want to say.
Thanks. Also, what's a good documentary on 1916 that I can show 15 year olds without them falling asleep? 45 minutes max.
Grand, I'll look up the RTÉ ones. Cheers.

Oh, and I almost forgot, Saoirse's school is doing a "Seachtain na Gaeilge" thing early and she has to write a short piece in Irish about her family. She asked me to check it and my Irish is... Leaving Cert pass level from 2002. Can you check this for obvious mistakes:

"Is mise Saoirse. Tá mé trí bliana déag d'aois. Tá deartháir amháin agam, Cian is ainm dó agus tá sé naoi mbliana d'aois. Tá sé an-chainteach agus bíonn sé ag imirt peile i gcónaí. Tá mo Dhaid ina mhúinteoir agus déanann sé troscán freisin. Tá cónaí orainn i nGaillimh. Tá mo Mham ina cónaí i mBaile Átha Cliath. Is maith liom ceol agus ag damhsa. Is breá liom mo mhadra ach níl madra againn."
Ha, the last line. "I love my dog but we don't have a dog." She's been campaigning for a dog for two years. That's a political statement, not a mistake. I'll leave it in.
And "ag damhsa" should be "damhsa" after "is maith liom", fair enough, I'll tell her. Night.
The letter from Corrib Lettings arrived. Uploading it. Rent's going up, surprise surprise.
Before you read it, ballpark: is 710 a month for a 60 square metre workshop unit in Galway outrageous or is it just that Pat was a saint? I've been paying 620.
Yeah, it's actually still below market for Galway these days. Pat was a saint. I'll stop moaning. Mostly.
Can you read through the lease letter and flag anything that might bite me? I'm a history teacher, not a solicitor, and the last lease I signed was with Pat on the back of a feed bag.

Right, so the rent and notice I knew about. The insurance requirement is fine, I have that. The access hours 7am to 10pm are grand for me. The bit about no spray finishing without approved extraction is the one I'll need to think about, I don't spray much but I've done the odd job with an HVLP gun with the door open. I'll keep that in mind.
And there's the bit about the 3 months notice from either side. So they could get rid of me with 3 months notice? Is that normal?
Yeah. Grand. Not ideal but normal for these small units. I'll sign it, I'm not moving the whole workshop, it took me a week to move the lathe in.
Should I reply to Sinéad with any questions before signing? I don't want to look like a pushover but I don't want a fight with a new landlord either.

Good: ask about the extraction spec (what counts as "approved"), whether the 710 is fixed for 2027, and who to contact for repairs now that Pat isn't around with his toolbox. Fair questions. Can you draft that email? Short and friendly.
Sound, sending that.
Different thing: Cian has a project on "a famous Irish invention" and he chose the ejector seat because "it's the coolest". Is it true that an Irish person invented the ejector seat?
James Martin from County Down, Martin-Baker. Cian's going to be insufferable about this. Grand. Give me three facts a 9 year old would love.
"It's saved over 7,000 lives" is a good one, he'll use that as his opening line, he loves a big number.
Right, that's me.
Bit of a ramble tonight, I'm thinking about the future and I've had a glass of wine.

So Driftwood is now making real money. Two big commissions at once, people asking about more. I'm wondering whether to go part-time at school next year, like a job share or three days a week, and give Driftwood two proper days. The kids are getting older, Saoirse's starting to need me less (or so she tells me, loudly).

But it's a big risk. Teaching is secure, pension, summers off with the kids. Driftwood is me, a lathe, and the goodwill of Galway's middle classes. I genuinely don't know. I haven't decided anything and I haven't said it to anyone at school.

Feb: 1 job (blanket box) - 350
Mar: nothing (exam season, no time)
Apr: 3 jobs (two chairs, a mirror frame) - 690
May: 1 porch bench (Joe & Sinéad) - 750
Jun: 2 jobs (dresser, side table) - 1,100

Aug: 3 jobs - 1,450

Expected: Cupán benches 1,950 in Nov, Kelly balance in Dec
Materials and costs so far this year roughly 2,900
Workshop rent 620/month

Right, so around 8,500 gross so far before the big two land, and after workshop rent and materials it's a lot less impressive. And most of it was in the summer when I had time. So if I had two days a week all year it could look different, but it's a guess.
The "test it before you jump" idea is good: track hours properly for the next six months and see what the hourly rate actually is. Will do. Still undecided though. Probably will be for a while.
Tax question while I'm at it. I've been declaring the Driftwood income on a Form 11 as a side income, my accountant handles it. Do I need to register for VAT at some point?
Grand, the threshold for services is well above what I'm making. Not a worry yet.

Also, completely random, but my brother Ger keeps sending me articles about how teachers are leaving the profession. Here's one he sent, is it accurate or is it scaremongering:

"Irish schools face growing teacher shortage
Principals across the country are reporting unprecedented difficulty in filling teaching posts, particularly in subjects such as Irish, home economics, physics, chemistry and modern languages. A survey of principals found that a large majority had unfilled vacancies at the start of the school year, and many schools have had to drop subjects or rely on unqualified substitute teachers. The shortage is attributed to several factors: the high cost of housing in urban areas, particularly Dublin, which makes it difficult for young teachers to live near their schools; the number of Irish teachers working abroad in the Middle East and Australia, where pay and conditions can be more attractive; and an increase in teachers taking career breaks or job-sharing. Unions have called for measures including housing supports for teachers, a faster route back for teachers abroad, and more flexible working arrangements. The Department of Education says it has increased the number of training places and introduced measures to allow student teachers to work as substitutes."

Ha, so it's broadly accurate, especially for certain subjects and Dublin. Geography and history aren't the shortage subjects, which means if I go part-time someone could fill my hours, which oddly makes me feel better about the idea.
Ok, enough navel gazing. Thanks for listening. Night.

Now, I've a parent email that I need help answering. I get one of these every year. Here it is:

"Dear Mr. O'Driscoll,
I received the letter about the Berlin trip and I have a number of concerns that I would like addressed before I consider allowing my son Darragh to attend. Firstly, the cost of 689 euro is very high, and I do not see why the school cannot organise a trip within Ireland which would be just as educational and a fraction of the price. Secondly, I am concerned about the visit to a concentration camp. Darragh is a sensitive boy and I do not think it is appropriate to expose 15 year olds to such distressing material. Thirdly, I have read reports about pickpocketing and crime in Berlin and I would like to know what security arrangements are in place, and what the ratio of teachers to students is. Fourthly, I would like to know if the students will be allowed any free time unsupervised, and if so, how much. Finally, I would like to know whether students who do not go on the trip will be penalised in any way in their TY assessment, because I do not think it is fair that a family's financial situation should affect a child's grades.
I look forward to your response.
Regards,
Fionnuala Hegarty"
To be fair to her, all of those are legitimate questions, she's just put them in a very cross way. I want to answer each point without being defensive.

That's very good. I like the bit on Sachsenhausen: that it's optional to walk certain parts, there's a pre-visit lesson, and the guide is trained for school groups. And yes, the ratio is 1 to 10 and there's no unsupervised free time, they're in groups of 4 minimum with check-in times in a defined area.

And the TY assessment bit: students not going do an alternative project in school, no penalty. And the school has a fund for families who need help with the cost, I should mention that more clearly. Can you make that paragraph a bit more prominent?
Sound. Sending it tomorrow after I sleep on it, never send a reply to a cross parent the same evening.
Unrelated: Driftwood question. I've an old Record No. 5 jack plane I bought at a car boot sale and the sole isn't flat. How do I flatten it without a machinist?
Sandpaper on a flat surface, glass or granite tile, marker on the sole to track progress, patience. Fine, a winter evening job.
Also what's a good grit progression for that?
Grand, 80 up to 220 or so for the sole, the iron is a separate job. Cheers.
Right, kids are fighting over the remote. Gotta go referee.

Ok, different. Here's something I want help with. Next week is Dad's anniversary, two years. My brothers and I are meeting for a pint in his local and I said I'd say a few words. I wrote this, it's a bit rough:

"So two years. Feels like longer and shorter at the same time. I was thinking about Dad today and what I keep coming back to is the walks. "THE BERLIN WALL (1961-1989)
After the Second World War ended in 1945, Germany was divided into four zones of occupation, controlled by the United States, Britain, France and the Soviet Union. In 1949, the three western zones became the Federal Republic of Germany (West Germany), a democracy allied with the United States, while the Soviet zone became the German Democratic Republic (East Germany), a communist state controlled by the Soviet Union. West Berlin became an island of the West surrounded by East Germany.

Throughout the 1950s, millions of East Germans fled to the West, many of them through Berlin, where crossing between sectors was relatively easy. By 1961, around 2.7 million people had left East Germany, including many young, skilled workers such as doctors, engineers and teachers. This 'brain drain' threatened to destroy the East German economy. On the night of 12-13 August 1961, East German soldiers and workers began to close the border, first with barbed wire and then with concrete. Families were separated overnight; some people woke up to find they could no longer go to work, school or visit relatives on the other side of the street.

Over the following years the wall was strengthened many times. By the 1980s it consisted of two walls with a 'death strip' between them, containing watchtowers, floodlights, dogs, trip-wire machine guns and trenches. Guards had orders to shoot anyone trying to escape. At least 140 people were killed trying to cross the Wall in Berlin. Despite this, around 5,000 people managed to escape, using tunnels, hot-air balloons, hidden compartments in cars, and even a zip line.

The Wall became the most famous symbol of the Cold War. In 1963, US President John F. Kennedy visited West Berlin and declared 'Ich bin ein Berliner' to show American support for the city. In 1987, President Ronald Reagan stood at the Brandenburg Gate and challenged the Soviet leader: 'Mr. Gorbachev, tear down this wall!'

By the late 1980s, the communist regimes in Eastern Europe were weakening. Hungary opened its border with Austria in 1989, and thousands of East Germans fled through it. Mass protests took place in East German cities, especially Leipzig, where hundreds of thousands of people marched peacefully every Monday shouting 'Wir sind das Volk' ('We are the people'). On the evening of 9 November 1989, an East German official, Günter Schabowski, announced at a press conference that East Germans could travel freely. Germany was officially reunified on 3 October 1990. Today, only a few sections of the Wall remain. On our trip we will visit the Berlin Wall Memorial at Bernauer Strasse, where you can see a preserved section of the death strip and learn about the people who lived along it and those who tried to escape."

"There's a particular kind of novel that Irish writers do better than anyone: the quiet book about a small place where nothing happens, except that everything does. Claire Keegan's 'Small Things Like These' is perhaps the best recent example, and the book I'm reviewing this week sits comfortably in that tradition, although it is a debut and occasionally shows it.

'The Weir Keeper' tells the story of Seán Daly, a man in his sixties who has spent forty years maintaining the old salmon weir on a river in Connemara. The weir is being decommissioned by a state agency, and Seán is given three months' notice. The novel follows those three months, as Seán continues to go down to the weir each morning, out of habit and stubbornness, while around him the village argues about tourism, fishing rights, wind turbines and a proposed greenway.

The book's greatest strength is its sense of place. The author, who grew up near Oughterard, knows the landscape intimately: the way the light changes on the lake in October, the particular smell of a turf fire in a damp kitchen, the silence of a village after the last pub closes. There are passages describing the river that I read twice, simply for the pleasure of the sentences.

Seán himself is a wonderful creation, a man who says very little but notices everything. His relationship with his estranged daughter, who returns from London midway through the novel, is handled with real delicacy. Their conversations are short, awkward, full of things not said, and utterly convincing to anyone who has grown up in an Irish family.

Where the book is weaker is in its secondary characters. The developer who wants to build holiday homes is a cardboard villain, and the young environmental activist who befriends Seán exists mainly to explain things to the reader. The middle section also drags, with several chapters that cover similar ground. A more ruthless editor might have cut fifty pages.

The ending, which I won't spoil, is quietly devastating, and earns its emotion honestly. It is not a happy ending, exactly, but it is a true one.

'The Weir Keeper' is not a perfect novel, but it is a deeply felt one, and it announces a writer of real talent. If you liked Keegan, or John McGahern, or Colm Tóibín's quieter books, you will find much to love here. It would make a good Christmas present for the kind of reader who likes to sit by the fire and be moved without being manipulated.

Four stars out of five."

Geography lesson planning again. My 5th years are doing climate change and the textbook section is out of date. A colleague sent me this summary from a report, can you turn it into 6 clear bullet points for students, and suggest a discussion question?

"Human influence has warmed the climate at a rate that is unprecedented in at least the last 2,000 years. Global surface temperature in the first two decades of the 21st century was about 1.1 degrees Celsius higher than in the period 1850-1900, and the increase is attributable to greenhouse gas emissions from human activities, principally the burning of fossil fuels and changes in land use. The effects are already observable across every region: more frequent and intense heatwaves, heavier precipitation events in many areas, more severe droughts in some regions, retreat of glaciers, reduction in Arctic sea ice, and rising sea levels, which have risen by about 20 cm since 1900 and are rising at an accelerating rate. Ireland is projected to experience wetter winters, drier summers in the east and south, increased coastal flooding and erosion, and more frequent extreme weather events such as storms. Limiting warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels would require rapid, deep and sustained reductions in greenhouse gas emissions, reaching net zero carbon dioxide emissions around the middle of the century. Every increment of warming increases the risks and the costs of adaptation. Options for mitigation include transitioning to renewable energy, improving energy efficiency, electrifying transport and heating, protecting and restoring forests and peatlands, and changing agricultural practices. Peatlands are particularly significant for Ireland: drained peatlands release large amounts of carbon dioxide, while rewetting them can turn them back into carbon stores."

Great bullets. The peatland one is great for Galway kids, half of them have a grandparent who cut turf. The discussion question "should Ireland stop cutting turf entirely, even for families who've done it for generations?" is going to cause a row. Which is the point.
Can you give me a case study on coastal erosion in Galway or the west of Ireland that I can use?
Grand, I know some of the Salthill prom stories myself from the storms, I'll use the 2014 storms when the prom flooded. Dad was out walking it the morning after, naturally.
Also, how do I handle the one kid in every class who says climate change is a hoax because his uncle said so? I don't want to humiliate him but I can't let it slide.
"Let's look at the evidence together" rather than "you're wrong". And ask what would change his mind. Good. Teaching, not winning.
Thanks. Different thing: what's a good, cheap, fishy dinner for three that I can make in 20 minutes on a Tuesday after training?
Salmon traybake with potatoes and broccoli, everything on one tray. Lovely. Cian will eat the broccoli if I call it "trees". He's 9, not stupid, he knows they're not trees, but he plays along.
Night.
Two emails today, one nice, one mad.

The nice one: Gráinne Walsh, the incoming principal, sent an introductory email to all staff ahead of starting in January. Here it is. Tell me what you read between the lines:

"Dear colleagues,
I hope this finds you well as the term settles in. Although I will not formally take up the role of principal until January, I wanted to introduce myself and say how much I am looking forward to joining the St. Enda's community. I have been very warmly welcomed by Mr. Hennessy, who has been generous with his time and his insights, and I am conscious that I will be following a principal who has served the school with great distinction for many years.
Over the coming months I hope to visit the school on a small number of occasions, with Mr. Hennessy's agreement, to meet staff informally and to get a sense of the rhythms and the culture of the school. I would genuinely welcome the opportunity to hear from as many of you as possible about what you value about St. Enda's, what you think works well, and what you would like to see change.
In my current school, I have found it helpful to use data, alongside professional judgement, to understand where students are thriving and where they may need more support. I want to reassure you that this is not about adding to anyone's workload or turning teaching into a spreadsheet. It is about making sure that we can see patterns that might otherwise be missed, so that we can support both students and staff more effectively.
I am also very interested in the extracurricular life of the school, including the trips, the sports, the arts and the many other activities that I know make St. Enda's special. I am aware that a number of significant events are planned for the second half of the year, and I look forward to supporting them.
In January, I will be inviting every member of staff to a short one-to-one conversation, at a time that suits you. In the meantime, please do not hesitate to contact me at this email address if there is anything you would like me to know.
With warm regards and best wishes for the term,
Gráinne Walsh"

Ha, so: "not about turning teaching into a spreadsheet" means there will be spreadsheets. But she's being careful and respectful of Tom, which I like. And the "significant events in the second half of the year" is the Berlin trip, she knows about it. Good. That's my opening for the courtesy email.

Now the mad one. Saoirse's class parents' WhatsApp group. I am the only dad in it who actually reads it. Here's what kicked off this evening:

"[19:02] Deirdre: Hi all, just a reminder that the class fundraiser bake sale is on Friday! Please send in baked goods with your child. Nut free please!! 🥜🚫
[19:04] Karen: Thanks Deirdre! Does it have to be homemade or can it be shop bought?
[19:05] Deirdre: Homemade preferred but shop bought is fine! Every bit helps 😊
[19:11] Michelle: Sorry who is organising the float for the bake sale? Last year there was no change and we lost loads of sales
[19:12] Deirdre: I think Aisling said she would?
[19:20] Aisling: I didn't say that 😅 I said I would do the tables
[19:21] Michelle: Well someone needs to do it
[19:25] Karen: I can't do Friday I'm working sorry
[19:33] Unknown number: Hi is this the 2nd year group for Ms. Kearney's class?
[19:34] Deirdre: No this is Mr. Daly's class 😊
[19:34] Unknown number: Sorry!!
[19:41] Michelle: Also can I just say, I don't think it's fair that the same five parents do everything every year
[19:43] Deirdre: Michelle I don't think that's helpful
[19:44] Michelle: I'm just saying what everyone is thinking
[19:52] Aisling: Can we maybe take this offline
[20:03] Karen: Has anyone else's child got the maths homework done, Cillian says he doesn't understand question 4
[20:05] Deirdre: Let's keep this group for class events please 🙏
[20:06] Michelle: 🙄"
Should I volunteer to do the float just to end this? I'm free Friday morning, I've a free class period first thing. Or will that make me the person who does the float forever?

Yeah, I'll offer to do the float THIS year, saying clearly "this year". And maybe suggest a rota sign-up sheet for next year, which takes the sting out of Michelle's point. Can you draft the message? Short, friendly, defuses things.

"Happy to do the float on Friday this year — I'll bring change from the bank. Maybe we could do a quick sign-up sheet for next year's events so the jobs get spread around? 🙂" Grand, that's diplomatic. I'll even put the emoji in, I'm adapting to my environment.
And for the bake sale itself, I can make something nut-free that's not a disaster? I'm a decent cook but a terrible baker.
Rice Krispie buns with chocolate. Can't go wrong. Saoirse will be mortified that I didn't do something more impressive, which is part of the fun.
Night.

Driftwood business stuff. There's a Christmas craft fair at the Galway Arts Centre in early December and the application asks a bunch of questions. I've drafted answers but they're all a bit "I like wood". Help me make them sound like a real business without sounding like a wanker:

"1. Tell us about your business (max 150 words).
Driftwood Restoration is a one-man furniture restoration business based in Galway. I restore old furniture, mainly Irish pieces from the 1900s to the 1970s, and also make some new pieces like benches and small tables. I've been doing this for about six years as a side business alongside my teaching job.

2. What will you be selling at the fair?
I will be selling some small restored pieces like stools, a blanket box and a few chairs. I will also have some new small items like chopping boards and coasters made from offcuts. And I'll have information about the restoration service.

3. What makes your work unique?
I try to keep as much of the original piece as possible. I use traditional methods like hide glue and French polish. I like to find out the history of the piece if I can.

4. Price range of items.
Coasters 8 euro for 4, chopping boards 25-45 euro, stools 80-150 euro, chairs 120-200 euro, blanket box 350 euro.

5. Do you have any sustainability practices?
I reuse old wood. The offcuts become chopping boards. Restoring furniture is better than buying new.

6. Space requirements.
One standard stall (2m x 1m table). No electricity needed.

7. Social media / website.
Instagram @driftwood.restoration.galway. No website yet."

That's so much better. The opening line "Every piece of old furniture has outlived someone who loved it. My job is to make sure it outlives the next person too." — that's a bit grand but I actually like it. It's true.
And in sustainability, adding the actual number, I estimated I've kept around 120 pieces out of landfill over 6 years, that's more convincing than "better than buying new".

The craft fair is on the 5th and 6th of December. The 6th is a Sunday. So I'd do Saturday only, if they allow that, or get one of my brothers to mind the stall on the Sunday. Is it normal to ask for one day only?
Grand, I'll ask. Ger owes me one anyway, he can do the Sunday. I'm not breaking the Sunday rule for coasters.
Pricing check: are my chopping board prices too low? They take me about 2 hours each including finishing.
Yeah, for end-grain boards that's too cheap. 45-65 for end grain, 25-35 for simple ones. I'll adjust.
Can you suggest a simple display layout for a 2m table? I want it to look good, not like a car boot sale.

Height at the back with the stools, chopping boards fanned in the middle, coasters at the front for the impulse buy, and a framed "before and after" photo of the Kelly sideboard when it's done. Love it. If Maeve ever sends me the fabric, the chairs could be in there too.
Night.
Quick round-up before the weekend, my head's full.
Declan's vetting still hasn't come through. Bríd says the ETB has "escalated it". Hannah at EuroStudy says she can hold the group fare for one more week. So Berlin's still stuck on that.
Maeve still hasn't sent the fabric. She went back to the shop on Saturday and "loved the teal but wanted to sleep on it". It's been four sleeps.
Cupán benches: first two coats this Saturday as planned. Then delivery on the 20th.

Ok, unrelated, my mother's Christmas cake recipe. I found her handwritten card in a drawer and I want to make it this year, first time since she passed. Some of it's hard to read and some of it is in "Mam measurements". Can you help me convert it?

"Mam's Christmas Cake
1 lb sultanas, 1 lb raisins, half lb currants, 4 oz cherries (wash them!!), 2 oz mixed peel
Soak all the fruit in a good glass of whiskey (not the good whiskey) overnight, or a few nights if you remember
half lb butter, half lb brown sugar, cream them till your arm is sore
5 eggs, one at a time, a spoon of the flour with each so it doesn't curdle
10 oz plain flour, 1 tsp mixed spice, half tsp cinnamon, a good grating of nutmeg, pinch of salt
2 oz ground almonds
grated rind of a lemon and an orange
Mix the fruit in last with a big spoon not the mixer
Line a 9 inch tin with two layers of brown paper and tie newspaper round the outside
Low oven (gas 2) for about 4 hours, test with a skewer, don't open the door for the first 2 hours or it'll sink and it'll be your own fault
Feed it with whiskey every week until Christmas (the cake not your father)"
Ha, "the cake not your father". That's her exactly. Ok so in grams and a fan oven temperature. Gas 2 is about 150C, so 130C fan. Got it.
Can I make it without the ground almonds? Cian's friend Rory has a nut allergy and he's here a lot over Christmas.

Grand, swap the ground almonds for the same weight of extra flour or a bit of breadcrumbs, and check the mixed peel and cherries for "may contain nuts" labels. Good shout. I'll make it nut-free and keep it safe.
When should I make it? It's October now.
End of October or early November gives it time to be fed. I'll do it the weekend after next. Not Sunday. Obviously. Saturday baking with the kids, Mam would like that.
Thanks. Right, Vanessa needs diesel and Cian needs a lift to training. Night.

A past student, Aoibheann, emailed asking me to write a reference for her application to study history and archaeology in Edinburgh. She was in my Leaving Cert class two years ago, took a gap year. She sent me her personal statement so I know what she's saying about herself. Can you read it and help me write a reference that complements it rather than repeating it?

"Ever since I found a clay pipe stem in my grandmother's garden in Clifden when I was nine, I have wanted to understand how ordinary people lived in the past. That small piece of white clay, probably dropped by a farm labourer in the nineteenth century, made me realise that history is not only about kings and battles but about people whose names were never written down.

At school, history was my favourite subject. I was particularly drawn to the social history of nineteenth-century Ireland, and for my Leaving Certificate research study I investigated the impact of the Famine on the Clifden workhouse, using the Board of Guardians minute books held in the county archives. Reading the handwritten records of admissions and deaths was an emotional experience, and it taught me how much can be learned from sources that were never intended for historians. My research study received an A grade.

During my gap year I volunteered for four months with a community archaeology project in Connemara, excavating a deserted pre-Famine village. I learned basic excavation techniques, how to record contexts and finds, and how to work as part of a team in difficult conditions, often in the rain. I was surprised by how much of archaeology is careful recording rather than discovery, but I found that I enjoyed the patience it requires. I also gave tours of the site to visiting school groups, which helped me develop confidence in explaining complex ideas simply.

I have also worked part-time in a café in Galway, which has taught me time management and how to deal with people, including difficult ones. In my free time I read widely, particularly social history and historical fiction, and I play the fiddle in a traditional music session every Thursday.

I am applying to study History and Archaeology because I want to combine the documentary evidence I enjoyed working with in school with the material evidence I discovered in the field. I am particularly interested in the archaeology of rural communities and how material culture can give a voice to people who left few written records. I hope to eventually work in heritage or research, perhaps focusing on the archaeology of the Irish diaspora.

Edinburgh's combination of strong historical and archaeological departments, and its fieldwork opportunities, make it the ideal place for me to pursue these interests."

Lovely statement. She was genuinely one of the best students I've had. Here's what I can add that she can't say about herself: she was the one who organised the class trip to the county archives for everyone else; she helped a struggling classmate with his research study without being asked; her research study was among the best I've marked in 16 years; and she argued with me, politely and with evidence, about the role of the Catholic Church in the Famine relief, and she was partly right.
That's great. Keep the bit about her arguing with me, universities love independent thinkers. Can you make it about 350 words, formal but warm? UK universities like a structured reference apparently.

Perfect. I'll sign it as "Mr. Liam O'Driscoll, Teacher of History and Geography, St. Enda's Community School". Should I mention I'm her former teacher only, or that I'm also the trip leader etc.? Doesn't matter really.
Grand, just subject teacher. Thanks.
Unrelated: the kids want to carve pumpkins for Halloween. Do they still do turnips in Ireland or is it all American pumpkins now? I want to tell them the history.

Right, turnips were the original Irish jack-o'-lanterns, terrifying things, and the pumpkin came back from America. I'll make them carve one turnip each as a history lesson, then they can have pumpkins. They'll hate me for about ten minutes.
And Samhain, the actual origin. Short version please, for a 9 and 13 year old.

Good. The thin veil between the living and the dead, bonfires, disguises so spirits wouldn't recognise you. Cian will want to dress up as a spirit. Saoirse will roll her eyes and then secretly dress up anyway.
Thanks. Night.

For my history society talk on 1920s Galway, I found an old newspaper report in the archives. It's dense and old-fashioned. Can you help me pull out the interesting human details I could use? Here's the transcription:

"GALWAY NOTES. The past week has been one of considerable activity in the city, notwithstanding the continued inclemency of the weather. The new picture house in Middle Street, which opened its doors to the public on Saturday evening last, was thronged to capacity, and it is reported that many persons were obliged to be turned away at the door. The programme consisted of an American drama of the West, together with a comic subject which provoked much laughter, and an orchestra of four performers provided musical accompaniment. The management announces that there will be a special matinee on Wednesday for the children of the city schools, at a reduced price of twopence. It is to be hoped that this new form of amusement will not draw the young people away from more improving pursuits.

At the Claddagh, the fishermen report poor catches for the season, the herring having failed to appear in their usual numbers. Several families are said to be in some distress, and the St. Vincent de Paul Society has made arrangements for the distribution of coal and provisions. A meeting of the fishermen was held on Thursday at which it was resolved to petition the Minister for Fisheries for assistance in the purchase of new nets and the repair of boats damaged in the storms of the previous month.

The County Council met on Tuesday, when the question of the Irish language in the schools of the county again occupied the members for a considerable time. Mr. Ó Flaithearta proposed that the Council should request the Department to ensure that teachers appointed to schools in the Irish-speaking districts be competent in the language, a proposal which was carried after a lengthy debate. Some members expressed concern that the requirement might cause difficulty in obtaining teachers.

On Sunday the annual excursion of the Galway Workmen's Club to Salthill took place, favoured, for once, by fine weather. Upwards of three hundred members and their families travelled by brake and on foot to the promenade, where sports were held for the children and a band played selections. The bathing was not largely availed of, the water being described by those who ventured in as 'very fresh'.

The price of eggs at Saturday's market was 1s 4d per dozen, butter 1s 8d per lb, and potatoes 6d per stone. Turf was plentiful."

Brilliant. The new cinema crowd turned away at the door, the hope that it "will not draw young people away from more improving pursuits" (ha, the 1920s version of worrying about phones), the herring failing in the Claddagh, the Irish teachers debate (which is still going on, basically), and people bathing at Salthill in "very fresh" water. Dad would've been one of them in a later decade.
Can you help me turn the prices into something modern people would understand? Like, what's 1s 4d for a dozen eggs relative to wages then?
Right, a labourer earning maybe 30-40 shillings a week, so eggs were a real cost. That's a nice way to show it, "a dozen eggs was about an hour's wages". Ok.
I'll use the "very fresh" line as my closing joke. A Galway audience will appreciate that nothing has changed in 100 years.
Different question: is "brake" in that article a type of carriage? I assume it's not a car brake.
Right, a large horse-drawn wagon for groups. Good, I'll explain that. Thanks, that was fun. Proper history nerd evening.
Night.

I'm mentoring a TY mini-company group this year (on top of everything else, because I can't say no). Four students, they want to sell upcycled furniture, which I suspect is why they picked me. Here's their business plan draft. Be honest but remember they're 15:

"BUSINESS PLAN - 'ReLove Furniture' (TY Mini Company, St. Enda's)
Team: Ciara (Managing Director), Oisín (Finance), Méabh (Marketing), Tadhg (Production)

1. Our idea: We will collect old furniture that people don't want, like chairs, small tables and stools, and upcycle them by sanding, painting them in bright colours and adding new handles or fabric. Then we will sell them at school events, at the Christmas craft fair and on Instagram. Our slogan is 'Old furniture, new love'.

2. Our market: Students' parents, teachers, young people moving into their first apartment, and people who care about the environment. Galway has a lot of students and young people who can't afford new furniture and like unique things.

3. Our competitors: IKEA (but our stuff is unique and more sustainable), charity shops (but our stuff is upcycled and nicer), and other upcycling people on Instagram (but we are students, so people will want to support us).

4. Getting furniture: We will ask our families, neighbours and teachers for unwanted furniture. We will also check the free section on DoneDeal and Facebook Marketplace.

5. Costs: Paint - 15 euro per tin, we think 6 tins = 90 euro. Sandpaper - 20 euro. Brushes - 25 euro. New handles - 2 euro each, maybe 30 handles = 60 euro. Fabric - 40 euro. Instagram ads - 30 euro. Transport - we will ask our parents. Total: 265 euro.

6. Prices: Chairs 35 euro, stools 25 euro, small tables 50 euro, bigger pieces 80+ euro.

7. Sales target: We want to sell 20 pieces by Easter, which would make about 800 euro.

8. Profit: 800 - 265 = 535 euro profit, which we will split between us and give 10% to Galway Simon Community.

9. Risks: We might not get enough furniture. Painting might take longer than we think. People might not buy. Someone might get hurt using tools.

10. Production: We will work in the school woodwork room on Wednesday afternoons with permission from Mr. Burke."

Agreed, it's a good start. Main gaps: they haven't counted their own time, transport is a big hidden cost ("ask our parents" is not a plan), they need a sanding/finishing safety plan with Mr. Burke, and the sales target might be optimistic given they can only work on Wednesdays. And their competitor section is a bit "we're nicer".
I like the idea of them doing a "test batch" of 3 pieces first, time how long each takes, and set prices from that. Real data, not guesses. Gráinne would approve, ha.
Can you write feedback in a format I can give them as a group, with 3 "what's great" and 3 "what to work on"? Keep the language encouraging.
Perfect. Also, should I let them use my van for collecting furniture? Probably not, insurance-wise?
Yeah, no, I'm not insured to transport students' business stock, and the school would have a fit. Parents with cars, with a sign-off form. Fine.

Different thing. I'm taking the kids to Dublin for a weekend in half-term, staying with my brother Ger, and I want to do one history thing with them that won't bore them. I'm thinking Kilmainham Gaol. Here's the info from the website, is it suitable for a 9 year old?

"Kilmainham Gaol - Visitor Information
Kilmainham Gaol is one of the largest unoccupied gaols in Europe. Built in 1796, it held many of the leaders of Irish rebellions, from the 1798 United Irishmen to the leaders of the 1916 Rising, fourteen of whom were executed in the Stonebreakers' Yard in May 1916. The gaol also held ordinary men, women and children, many imprisoned for petty crimes such as stealing food during the Great Famine. Some prisoners were as young as seven years old.
Access to the gaol is by guided tour only, lasting approximately one hour, followed by self-guided access to the museum exhibition. The tour includes the chapel, the old West Wing with its narrow cells, the Victorian East Wing (featured in many films), and the Stonebreakers' Yard where the 1916 executions took place.
Tours are suitable for all ages; however, some content deals with themes of imprisonment, hardship and execution, which parents may wish to discuss with younger children beforehand. Parts of the gaol are cold and dimly lit, and visitors are advised to wear warm clothing.
Tickets must be booked online in advance and tours frequently sell out, particularly at weekends and during school holidays. Admission: Adult EUR 8, Child EUR 4, Family ticket (2 adults and up to 3 children) EUR 20. Under-12s must be accompanied by an adult.
Getting here: Kilmainham Gaol is located approximately 3.5 km west of Dublin city centre. Luas Red Line to Suir Road (10-minute walk) or Dublin Bus routes 13, 40 and 69."

Grand, so suitable but I'll prep Cian beforehand, especially the bit about children being imprisoned for stealing food. That'll actually land with him, he's a big believer in fairness. And book online, holidays sell out.
Saoirse will want to see the East Wing because it's in some film she's seen. Fine, a hook's a hook.
And something fun after so it doesn't end on executions. Ideas nearby?
The Phoenix Park and the zoo, perfect, it's a bus ride away. History in the morning, giraffes in the afternoon, chips on the way home. That's a well-balanced day.
Should I book the Saturday or Sunday? Ger's working Saturday morning.
Saturday it is, just me and the kids, and Ger can meet us at the zoo after. And Sunday we're doing nothing but lying on Ger's couch. Thanks, sorted.
Night.

Quick one before bed. Saoirse asked me why Galway is called "the City of the Tribes" and I gave her the short version, but she wants the proper story for a school project. Can you give me the key points?

Right, the fourteen merchant families who dominated the town's trade and politics from the medieval period, the Lynches, Blakes, Frenchs and the rest, and Cromwell's forces using "tribes" as an insult that the families then adopted with pride. That's a nice twist for a 13 year old: taking an insult and making it a badge.
And the Lynch Memorial Window story, the mayor who supposedly hanged his own son? Is that true or a legend?

Grand, so it's a legend with very shaky evidence, and the word "lynching" almost certainly doesn't come from it, whatever the tour guides say. Good. I'll tell her to present it as a legend and say why historians doubt it. That's proper history.

Re: Unit 6, Ballybane Craft Yard - Notice of change of ownership and renewal of tenancy

Dear Mr. O'Driscoll,

As you may be aware, Ballybane Craft Yard was acquired by Corrib Lettings Ltd from Mr. Patrick Flaherty with effect from 1 September 2026. We are writing to all existing occupiers to formalise their tenancies under a written licence agreement. The key terms of your renewed tenancy are set out below. A full agreement will follow for signature.

1. Premises: Unit 6 (approx. 60 m2 workshop with mezzanine store), together with shared use of the yard for loading.

2. Term: Rolling monthly tenancy commencing 1 October 2026, terminable by either party on three (3) months' written notice.

3. Rent: The rent will remain at EUR 620 per month until 31 December 2026. From 1 January 2027 the rent will be EUR 710 per month, payable monthly in advance by standing order on the 1st of each month. Rent will be reviewed annually thereafter.

4. Service charge: A yard service charge of EUR 35 per month will apply from 1 January 2027, covering yard lighting, bin collection and maintenance of the shared access road.

5. Permitted use: Craft workshop and light industrial use (woodworking, furniture restoration and similar). Retail sales from the unit are not permitted, except by appointment.

6. Hours of access: The yard gate will be open from 7:00 to 22:00, seven days a week. Access outside these hours by prior arrangement only.

7. Finishing and fumes: Spray application of lacquers, paints, stains or other finishes is not permitted within the unit unless an extraction system approved in writing by the Landlord is installed and maintained. Brush, rag and wax application of finishes is permitted. Flammable materials must be stored in a metal cabinet.

8. Insurance: The occupier must hold public liability insurance of at least EUR 2.6 million and contents insurance, and provide a copy of the policy schedule annually.

9. Alterations: No structural alterations or new electrical installations without prior written consent.

10. Repairs: The Landlord is responsible for the roof, external walls and yard surfaces. The occupier is responsible for internal repairs and decoration. Repair requests should be emailed to repairs@corriblettings.ie.

11. Deposit: Your existing deposit held by Mr. Flaherty (EUR 620) has been transferred to us and will continue to be held as security.

Please confirm your acceptance of these terms by return email by 15 October 2026. We look forward to working with you.

Yours sincerely,
Sinéad Moran
